THE UPGRADE SCREEN IS A CONTROLLED A/B. It shows every readout for the
installed part AND for the alternative, side by side, with no tune drift
between the two halves. Nothing has to be bought to read it. Five pages
cycle with Toggle; page 1 (the six star ratings) is the only one not worth
capturing, because those are rounded to one decimal and derived from the
real numbers, and the PI appears on page 2 anyway.
So far this file holds the BASELINE ROW only — the car as it stands, with
the upgraded front track width installed. The stock-width halves are what
screen: upgrade menu — part preview, pages 2 to 5

thePreviewSHOWSTHEDEFAULTTUNE: AN OPEN QUESTION, CLOSED BY THIS BASELINE. When the Civic's upgrade-screen
readings came in, its Mechanical Balance matched neither the default-tune
reading nor the live one, so the fixture recorded that the preview is
'computed at some tune state of its own' and warned that only DELTAS were
usable.
The GR86 baseline settles it three ways at once:
readout            preview     tuning menu, default tune
Mech. Balance        0.50          0.50
Aero Balance         0.45          0.45
Aero Efficiency      0.750         0.75
Three for three, and the car's LIVE tune at the time was nothing like its
default. So the preview shows the game's DEFAULT TUNE for the previewed
configuration, not whatever is currently dialled in.
THE ONE LOOSE END, recorded rather than smoothed over: the Civic's preview
read 0.46 where its default-tune tuning-menu reading was 0.47. One printing
step, on one readout, on one car, against three exact matches here. Most
likely a rounding difference between two code paths, but it is not
explained and it is not being explained away.
WHY IT MATTERS: it means every upgrade-screen A/B is directly comparable to
a default-tune reading, so the parts group and the balance group share a
reference point rather than living in separate worlds. It also means the
screen can be read WITHOUT restoring the default tune first, which is the
step whose absence caused the SPREAD disaster.
twoCarsSideBySide: Both at A 700, both AWD, so the differences are the cars and the parts.
Nothing is concluded from this — two cars differing in tires, aero and
everything else is not an experiment. It is here because it is the first
time two complete, comparable rows have existed at all, and because two of
the differences are worth a second look later: the GR86 brakes 8 ft better
and corners harder on semi-slicks, and gives up 25 mph of top speed at a
much worse aero efficiency, which is what a downforce build looks like.

m10CONFIRMED: M10 HOLDS ON THE SECOND CAR, BOTH DIRECTIONS.
widen FRONT      widen REAR
Same signs and the same magnitudes: +0.02 at the front, -0.02 at the rear,
on two cars 571 lb apart with different tires, different aero and a 0.04
difference in baseline MB.
So Mechanical Balance is the rear axle's share of lateral LOAD TRANSFER.
Track divides. The roll-stiffness reading (track squared) and the
track-linear reading both get both signs wrong on both cars — four
independent chances to be right and they miss all four.
Aero balance and aero efficiency did not move on any width row, on either
car, which is the control this needed: the width upgrade is not quietly
doing something aerodynamic.
AND THE MAGNITUDES ARE STILL NOT QUOTABLE. The implied widening comes out
at 8.3-8.4% on all four rows, which looks like agreement to three digits
and is not: propagating the two-decimal rounding gives [4.1%, 12.8%] for
every one of them. Four overlapping intervals is a real consistency check.
Four point estimates that agree is where three roundings happened to fall.
What this earns: the app's standing note that 'the readout sees the wider
track and the formula does not, so trust the readout' can now say WHICH
WAY on any car. Widen the front, MB rises; widen the rear, MB falls.

widebodyIsPerKit: *** THIS WITHDRAWS A CLAIM PUBLISHED ONE COMMIT EARLIER. ***
The Civic's kit was measured first and read as a downforce kit: lateral G
up hard at speed, aero balance swinging 0.17, straight-line speed traded
away. The conclusion written was 'the widebody is a downforce kit'.
The GR86's Rocket Bunny kit does the opposite:
GR86 Rocket Bunny     Civic FH6 kit
One kit adds downforce and buys cornering speed with straight-line speed.
The other loses grip at BOTH speeds, brakes 5.8 ft worse, and gives up 40
PI for the privilege. They are not the same kind of part and there is no
general statement about 'widebodies' to be made.
THE LIKELY MECHANISM, UNCONFIRMED: the GR86's weight field is flagged red,
which means it went up. If the Rocket Bunny kit is heavy, every one of
those numbers follows without needing an aero story at all — grip, braking,
acceleration and top speed all degrade together, which is the signature of
mass rather than drag. The Civic's kit added 2 lb. One legible weight
reading settles it.
A SECOND READING, ALSO UNCONFIRMED: the GR86 already runs an aggressive
aero build — efficiency 0.750 against the Civic's 0.822, and a large wing.
A kit that adds downforce to a car that already has plenty would show much
less than one that adds it to a car that has none.
The lesson is the ordinary one and it keeps costing the same amount: a part
measured on one car describes that car and that part. The Civic reading was
not wrong; it was scoped as a rule when it was an observation.
